subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 10! In this unit you will become confident and accurate at multiplying and dividing large numbers. You already know your times tables and how to multiply small numbers. Now you will learn efficient written methods that let you handle numbers in the thousands, multiply by two-digit numbers, carry out long division, and even multiply and divide decimals. You will also learn how the order of operations decides which calculation to do first when several are written together.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Multiply numbers up to four digits by a single-digit number using the standard written method.
Multiply by multiples of 10 (such as 20, 30, 700) using place-value patterns.
Multiply a three-digit or four-digit number by a two-digit number (long multiplication).
Use the grid method as a second way to multiply and to check your work.
Carry out long division of large numbers, expressing remainders correctly.
Multiply and divide decimals by whole numbers.
Apply the correct order of operations (brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −).
Estimate products and quotients by rounding to check that answers are reasonable.
Solve multi-step word problems and check answers using inverse operations.
Use divisibility tests for 2, 4, 5, 10, 25 and 100 to check quickly whether one number divides exactly into another.
Use mental strategies for multiplication and division, including multiplying multiples of 10 and 100, adjusting from a near multiple, halving and doubling, and deriving new facts from known ones.

concepts.title: Multiplying Large Numbers by a Single Digit
concepts.explanation:
When you multiply a large number by a single digit, you use the standard written method (sometimes called the standard algorithm). You multiply one digit at a time, working from right to left, and you carry whenever a product is bigger than 9. The whole method rests on place value: the ones, tens, hundreds and thousands must each stay in their own column.

Let us work through 1347 × 8 carefully, one column at a time.

Step 1 – Estimate first. Round 1347 to 1000: 1000 × 8 = 8000. Round it up to 1500: 1500 × 8 = 12,000. So a correct answer must lie between 8000 and 12,000. Keep that range in mind.

Step 2 – Ones. 7 × 8 = 56. Write the 6 in the ones column and carry the 5 into the tens column.

Step 3 – Tens. 4 × 8 = 32, then add the carried 5 to get 37. Write the 7 in the tens column and carry the 3.

Step 4 – Hundreds. 3 × 8 = 24, add the carried 3 to get 27. Write the 7 in the hundreds column and carry the 2.

Step 5 – Thousands. 1 × 8 = 8, add the carried 2 to get 10. There are no more digits to multiply, so write the whole 10. The finished answer is 10,776.

Step 6 – Check against the estimate. Our answer 10,776 sits neatly between 8000 and 12,000, so it is reasonable. This checking step takes only a moment and catches most mistakes.

Carrying is just exchanging in place value. When 7 × 8 = 56, we have 56 ones. But only one digit fits in the ones column, so we exchange 50 of those ones for 5 tens: 56 ones = 5 tens + 6 ones. We write the 6 and carry the 5 into the tens column. It is exactly like changing 50 single shillings for five ten-shilling notes at the market – the value is the same, it is just grouped more tidily.
concepts.example: Here are two more to study. 2456 × 7: estimate 2500 × 7 = 17,500; the exact answer is 17,192, close to the estimate. 5089 × 6: estimate 5000 × 6 = 30,000; the exact answer is 30,534, again close. Notice how the estimate and the answer always end up the same size – that agreement is your safety net.

concepts.title: Multiplying by Multiples of 10, 100 and 1000
concepts.explanation:
Multiplying by 10, 100 or 1000 follows a beautiful place-value pattern. When you multiply by 10, every digit moves one place to the left and a 0 fills the empty ones column: 23 × 10 = 230. Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places left: 23 × 100 = 2300. Multiplying by 1000 moves them three places: 23 × 1000 = 23,000.

It is tempting to say “just add a zero”, but a careful mathematician thinks about why it works: the digits are sliding into bigger place-value columns, and the zero is a place holder that keeps them there. This matters enormously once you meet decimals, where “adding a zero” gives the wrong answer.

To multiply by other multiples of 10 – like 20, 30 or 700 – you split the multiple. For example, 20 = 2 × 10, so multiply by 2 and then by 10:

23 × 20 = 23 × 2 × 10 = 46 × 10 = 460

23 × 30 = 23 × 3 × 10 = 69 × 10 = 690

23 × 40 = 23 × 4 × 10 = 92 × 10 = 920

Let us use this on a larger number, 1234 × 30. First multiply 1234 × 3 = 3702, then multiply by 10 to get 37,020. In the written column method this is why the second line of a long multiplication ends in a 0 – you are really multiplying by a multiple of 10.
concepts.example: Real-life multiples of 10 are everywhere. Amina’s heart beats 72 times each minute, so in one hour (60 minutes) it beats 72 × 60 = 72 × 6 × 10 = 432 × 10 = 4320 times. A sheet of stamps holds 50 stamps, so 24 sheets hold 50 × 24 = 1200 stamps. Recognising a multiple of 10 in a problem lets you calculate in your head where others reach for a pencil.

concepts.title: Long Multiplication (Two-Digit Multipliers)
concepts.explanation:
When both numbers have two or more digits, you multiply in parts and then add the parts together. Each part is called a partial product. There are two popular methods, and it is worth knowing both: the grid method shows clearly what is happening, and the column method is quicker once you understand it.

The grid method breaks each number into its place-value parts. For 23 × 47, split 23 into 20 + 3 and 47 into 40 + 7, then fill a grid:

Now add all four partial products: 800 + 140 + 120 + 21 = 1081. Every part is visible, so it is easy to see nothing has been missed.

In the column method you multiply 23 by the ones digit (7), then by the tens digit (40), and add:

23 × 7 = 161 (first partial product)

23 × 40 = 920 (second partial product – notice it ends in 0)
concepts.example: The two methods always agree – that is the whole point of learning both. Try 156 × 24. By the grid method: 100×20 + 50×20 + 6×20 + 100×4 + 50×4 + 6×4 = 2000 + 1000 + 120 + 400 + 200 + 24 = 3744. By the column method: 156 × 4 = 624, and 156 × 20 = 3120, and 624 + 3120 = 3744. Same answer, two routes – a perfect way to check.

concepts.title: Long Division
concepts.explanation:
Let us divide 4356 ÷ 12. First estimate: 12 × 300 = 3600 and 12 × 400 = 4800, so the answer is between 300 and 400.

Divide: 12 does not go into 4, so look at 43. 43 ÷ 12 = 3 (because 3 × 12 = 36). Write 3 above the 3 of 43.

Multiply and subtract: 3 × 12 = 36; 43 − 36 = 7.

Bring down the next digit (5) to make 75. 75 ÷ 12 = 6 (because 6 × 12 = 72). Write 6. Then 75 − 72 = 3.

Bring down the last digit (6) to make 36. 36 ÷ 12 = 3 exactly (3 × 12 = 36). Write 3. Then 36 − 36 = 0.

The quotient is 363 with no remainder. Check by multiplying back: 363 × 12 = 4356. It matches the dividend, so the answer is correct. That multiply-back is the most powerful check in all of division.

Not every division comes out exactly. Consider 2345 ÷ 23. Working through the cycle gives 101 with 22 left over, written 101 remainder 22 (or 101 r22). Check: 23 × 101 = 2323, and 2323 + 22 = 2345, which is correct. Always confirm the remainder is smaller than the divisor – if it is not, the last quotient digit was too small.
concepts.example: How you treat a remainder depends on the problem. If 34 books are packed 5 to a box, then 34 ÷ 5 = 6 remainder 4: you need a 7th box for the last 4 books, so you round up. But if you are sharing 34 sweets equally among 5 children, each gets 6 and 4 are left over – here you keep the remainder as it is. Reading the question carefully tells you whether to round up, round down, or keep the remainder.

concepts.title: Multiplying and Dividing Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Money and measurements are full of decimals, so you must be able to multiply and divide them by whole numbers. The good news is that you use exactly the same written methods – you simply keep track of the decimal point.

To multiply a decimal by a whole number, ignore the decimal point at first, multiply as usual, then put the point back so the answer has the same number of decimal places as the decimal you started with. For example, 3.6 × 7: work out 36 × 7 = 252, then – because 3.6 has one decimal place – the answer has one decimal place: 25.2. A quick estimate (4 × 7 = 28) confirms 25.2 is about right.

A real example: a litre of camel milk costs 3.6 dollars at the Hargeisa market (we will use dollars for a tidy decimal). Seven litres cost 3.6 × 7 = $25.20. Notice we write money to two decimal places, so 25.2 becomes 25.20.

To divide a decimal by a whole number, divide as usual and keep the decimal point in the answer directly above the point in the number you are dividing. For example, 25.2 ÷ 7 = 3.6. You can see this is just the inverse of the multiplication above, which is a neat way to check. Another: 8.4 ÷ 4 – line up the point, divide 84 ÷ 4 = 21, keep one decimal place, giving 2.1.
concepts.example: The key idea is that the decimal point never moves during these calculations – you only make sure it stays lined up. The digits do the work; the point simply marks where the whole numbers end and the fractions of one begin.

concepts.title: Order of Operations
concepts.explanation:
What is the value of 6 + 3 × 4? If you work from left to right you might say 9 × 4 = 36, but that is wrong. Mathematicians all over the world agree to do multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, so 3 × 4 = 12 is done first, then 6 + 12 = 18. Without an agreed order, the same calculation would give different answers to different people – so the order of operations is a shared rule that keeps everyone in step.

I – Indices (powers), such as squaring.

D and M – Division and Multiplication, worked left to right.

A and S – Addition and Subtraction, worked left to right.
concepts.example: Brackets always come first because they let you override the normal order. Compare these two: 6 + 3 × 4 = 6 + 12 = 18, but (6 + 3) × 4 = 9 × 4 = 36. The brackets change which calculation happens first, and so they change the answer completely. Another example: 20 − 12 ÷ 4 = 20 − 3 = 17, because the division is done before the subtraction.

concepts.title: Divisibility Tests
concepts.explanation: A divisibility test is a quick way to check whether a number divides exactly by another number, without doing the full division. These tests save time and help you check answers, simplify fractions, and find factors quickly. A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even (0, 2, 4, 6 or 8) — for example, 738 is divisible by 2 because it ends in 8. A number is divisible by 5 if its last digit is 0 or 5 — for example, 645 is divisible by 5. A number is divisible by 10 if its last digit is 0 — for example, 970 is divisible by 10. A number is divisible by 100 if its last two digits are both 0 — for example, 4,300 is divisible by 100. A number is divisible by 4 if the number formed by its last two digits is divisible by 4 — for example, 3,516 is divisible by 4 because 16 ÷ 4 = 4 exactly. A number is divisible by 25 if its last two digits form 00, 25, 50 or 75 — for example, 2,675 is divisible by 25 because it ends in 75.
concepts.example: Test whether 6,384 is divisible by 2, 4, 5, 10, 25 or 100. Divisible by 2? Yes — it ends in 4, which is even. Divisible by 4? Check the last two digits, 84: 84 ÷ 4 = 21 exactly, so yes. Divisible by 5? No — it does not end in 0 or 5. Divisible by 10? No — it does not end in 0. Divisible by 25? No — the last two digits, 84, are not 00, 25, 50 or 75. Divisible by 100? No — the last two digits are not both 0. So 6,384 is divisible by 2 and 4, but not by 5, 10, 25 or 100.

concepts.title: Mental Multiplication and Division Strategies
concepts.explanation: Skilled mental mathematicians use a toolkit of strategies instead of always reaching for a written method. Four strategies are especially useful for multiplication and division. First, multiplying two multiples of 10 or 100: multiply the non-zero digits together, then attach all the zeros afterwards. For 40 × 500, multiply 4 × 5 = 20, then attach the total three zeros from 40 and 500 (one from 40, two from 500) to get 20,000. Second, the near-multiple strategy: if one number is close to an easy multiple of 10, calculate with the easy number first, then adjust. For 19 × 6, since 19 is one less than 20, calculate 20 × 6 = 120, then subtract one extra group of 6: 120 − 6 = 114. Third, the halve-and-double strategy: for a multiplication, you can double one number and halve the other without changing the answer, which sometimes turns an awkward calculation into an easy one. For 15 × 16, halve 16 to 8 and double 15 to 30, giving the easier calculation 30 × 8 = 240 (the same answer as 15 × 16). Fourth, generating new facts from known facts: once you know one multiplication or division fact, you can derive related facts by scaling. If you know 7 × 8 = 56, you instantly also know 70 × 8 = 560 (multiply one side by 10), 7 × 80 = 560, 56 ÷ 8 = 7, and 56 ÷ 7 = 8, without recalculating from scratch.
concepts.example: Use the near-multiple strategy to find 29 × 7 mentally: 29 is one less than 30, so calculate 30 × 7 = 210, then subtract one extra group of 7: 210 − 7 = 203. Now use halve-and-double to find 25 × 14: halve 14 to get 7, and double 25 to get 50, giving 50 × 7 = 350 (the same as 25 × 14). Finally, use a known fact to generate a new one: knowing 9 × 6 = 54, find 90 × 6 instantly by multiplying by 10: 90 × 6 = 540.

methods.title: Long multiplication (3-digit × 2-digit)
steps: Estimate first by rounding both numbers.
Multiply by the ones digit to get the first partial product.
Write a 0 in the ones column, then multiply by the tens digit for the second partial product.
Add the two partial products.
Compare with your estimate to check the size.

methods.title: Long division
steps: Estimate the quotient by rounding.
Divide the divisor into the digits from the left.
Multiply, then subtract, then bring down the next digit.
Repeat divide, multiply, subtract, bring down until no digits remain.
Write any remainder, then check by multiplying the quotient by the divisor.

methods.title: Multiplying or dividing a decimal by a whole number
steps: Ignore the decimal point and calculate with whole numbers.
Count the decimal places in the original decimal.
Put the point back so the answer has the same number of decimal places.
For division, keep the point in the answer directly above the point in the dividend.

methods.title: Long division, exact
steps: 16 into 14 will not go, so use 145.
Bring down 6 to make 16.
16 ÷ 16 = 1 exactly.

methods.title: Long division with a remainder
steps: 34 into 36 goes once (34), remainder 2.
Bring down 7 to make 27; 34 into 27 will not go, so write 0 and bring down 8 to make 278.
Quotient 108 remainder 6.

methods.title: Multiplying a decimal
methods.example: A litre of oil costs 4.5 dollars. What do 8 litres cost?
steps: Ignore the point: 45 × 8 = 360.
There is one decimal place in 4.5, so the answer has one decimal place: 36.0, i.e.
Estimate 4 × 8 = 32 confirms the size.

workedExamples.title: Single-digit multiplication
workedExamples.solution: Estimate 2500 × 7 = 17,500. Ones: 6×7 = 42, write 2 carry 4. Tens: 5×7 = 35, +4 = 39, write 9 carry 3. Hundreds: 4×7 = 28, +3 = 31, write 1 carry 3. Thousands: 2×7 = 14, +3 = 17, write 17. Answer 17,192, close to the estimate. ✓

workedExamples.title: Multiplying by a multiple of 10
workedExamples.solution: 1234 × 3 = 3702, then × 10 gives 37,020. Estimate 1000 × 30 = 30,000, so 37,020 is a sensible size. ✓

workedExamples.title: Long multiplication
workedExamples.solution: 234 × 6 = 1404 (first partial product). 234 × 50 = 11,700 (second partial product, ending in 0). Add: 1404 + 11,700 = 13,104. Estimate 200 × 60 = 12,000, so 13,104 is reasonable. ✓

workedExamples.title: Long division, exact
workedExamples.solution: 16 into 14 will not go, so use 145. 145 ÷ 16 = 9 (9×16 = 144), remainder 1. Bring down 6 to make 16. 16 ÷ 16 = 1 exactly. Quotient 91. Check: 91 × 16 = 1456. ✓

workedExamples.title: Long division with a remainder
workedExamples.solution: 34 into 36 goes once (34), remainder 2. Bring down 7 to make 27; 34 into 27 will not go, so write 0 and bring down 8 to make 278. 278 ÷ 34 = 8 (8×34 = 272), remainder 6. Quotient 108 remainder 6. Check: 34 × 108 = 3672, and 3672 + 6 = 3678. ✓

workedExamples.title: Multiplying a decimal
workedExamples.prompt: A litre of oil costs 4.5 dollars. What do 8 litres cost?
workedExamples.solution: Ignore the point: 45 × 8 = 360. There is one decimal place in 4.5, so the answer has one decimal place: 36.0, i.e. $36.00. Estimate 4 × 8 = 32 confirms the size. ✓

workedExamples.title: Order of operations
workedExamples.solution: Brackets first: 8 − 3 = 5. Then multiply: 6 × 5 = 30. Then add: 5 + 30 = 35. ✓

workedExamples.title: A two-step problem
workedExamples.prompt: Yusuf buys 24 boxes of dates with 36 dates in each box. He shares them equally among 8 families. How many dates does each family receive?
workedExamples.solution: First multiply: 24 × 36 = 864 dates in total. Then divide: 864 ÷ 8 = 108 dates per family. Check: 108 × 8 = 864. ✓

activities.title: Market Trader Challenge
activities.materials: paper, pencil, and small stones or bottle caps as ‘shillings’.
steps: Set up a pretend Hargeisa market stall with five goods and a price for each (for example, mangoes at 45 shillings, a bag of rice at 234 shillings).
A customer buys several of one item – say 30 mangoes. Work out the cost using multiplication by a multiple of 10.
Now the customer pays with a large note. Use division to work out the change.
Swap roles and repeat. Keep a written record of every calculation and check each one with an estimate.
This activity turns the whole unit into a game and shows how traders use multiplication and division every single day.

activities.title: Heartbeat Investigation
activities.materials: a clock or timer, and paper.
steps: Measure your resting heart rate: count your pulse for one minute.
Multiply by 60 to find beats per hour, then by 24 to find beats per day.
Multiply by 365 to estimate beats in a year – a huge number! Estimate first, then calculate.
Compare results with family members. Whose heart beats most in a day? Show your working.

activities.title: Grid-Method Art
activities.materials: squared paper, a ruler and coloured pencils.
steps: Choose a long-multiplication question such as 156 × 43.
Draw a large grid and split each number into place-value parts (100 + 50 + 6 and 40 + 3).
Fill each box with its partial product and colour boxes of equal value the same colour.
Add the partial products, then check your total using the column method. Do the two answers match?

activities.title: Long-Division Relay (Family or Group Game)
activities.materials: two or more players, paper and pencils.
steps: One player writes a long-division question, such as 3678 ÷ 34.
Players take turns to do ONE step each of the cycle: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
If a player makes a mistake, the next player must spot and fix it before carrying on.
Finish by multiplying the quotient back to check. The team wins if the check matches!

activities.title: BIDMAS Puzzle Maker
activities.materials: paper, pencil, and the digits 2, 3, 4 and 5.
steps: Using the four digits once each, with any operations and brackets, try to make the number 20 exactly.
Write down your calculation and check it obeys the order of operations.
Now try to make 14, then 30. How many different targets can you hit?
Give a friend one of your puzzles and see if they can find the same answer.

activities.title: Real-World Estimation Hunt
activities.materials: a notebook and your everyday surroundings.
steps: Find three real quantities to estimate: for example, how many litres of water your family uses in a week, or how many dates are in a full box.
Write a sensible estimate for each using rounding.
Where you can, find the exact number and compare it with your estimate.
Reflect: which estimates were closest, and how could you estimate better next time?

rules.title: Order of Operations (BIDMAS)
rules.text: What is the value of 6 + 3 × 4? If you work from left to right you might say 9 × 4 = 36, but that is wrong. Mathematicians all over the world agree to do multiplication and division before addition and subtraction, so 3 × 4 = 12 is done first, then 6 + 12 = 18. Without an agreed order, the same calculation would give different answers to different people – so the order of operations is a shared rule that keeps everyone in step.

rules.title: Division and Multiplication Share Equal Rank
rules.text: that division and multiplication share the same rank, so you work them left to right, not division-before-multiplication. The same is true for addition and subtraction. Getting this right matters more and more as you move towards algebra, where the order of operations is used in every single line.

I can multiply by multiples of 10 (such as 20, 30, 700) using place-value patterns.
I can multiply a three-digit or four-digit number by a two-digit number (long multiplication).
I can use the grid method as a second way to multiply and to check your work.
I can carry out long division of large numbers, expressing remainders correctly.
I can multiply and divide decimals by whole numbers.
I can apply the correct order of operations (brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −).
I can estimate products and quotients by rounding to check that answers are reasonable.
I can solve multi-step word problems and check answers using inverse operations.
